desc:
A magic block is a 3 × 3 square of neighbouring cells that contains each of the numbers 1 to 9 exactly once, and in which all three rows, all three columns and both diagonals have the same sum.

Given a rectangular grid of small non-negative integers, return how many 3 × 3 blocks of the grid are magic. Blocks may overlap.

grid = [[4,3,8,4],
        [9,5,1,9],
        [2,7,6,2]]  →  1

The left block is magic (all lines add up to 15). The right block is not: its main diagonal is 3 + 1 + 2.
hints: There are only (rows - 2) × (cols - 2) blocks. Check each one in constant time.
If the nine cells are 1..9, they add up to 45, so every line of a magic block must add up to 15.

The four lines through the centre (middle row, middle column, both diagonals) cover every cell once, except the centre which is counted four times. So 4 · 15 = 45 + 3 · centre, hence the centre must be 5. Use that as a cheap filter, then test the digits and the eight line sums.
editorial: Slide a 3 × 3 window over the grid and test it. A block qualifies when its nine values are exactly 1..9 (sorting them and comparing is enough) and the three rows, three columns and two diagonals share one sum. With nine distinct digits from 1..9 the total is 45, which forces that common sum to be 15.

A small observation speeds up the scan: adding the middle row, middle column and both diagonals counts every cell once and the centre four times, so 60 = 45 + 3 · centre and the centre has to be 5. Most windows are rejected by that single comparison. The work is O(rows · cols) with a constant of nine cells per window.
